**Rime** is a daily allocator. Each morning it splits capital between leveraged Nasdaq
ETF exposure, a volatility hedge, and cash. It's been running on Alpaca since April
2026.

Most of the work went into the plumbing rather than the signal — making sure the code
running in production is the same code that produced the backtest.

```{=html}
<div class="metrics">
<div class="metric"><div class="metric-value">1.86</div><div class="metric-label">Sharpe, simulated</div><div class="metric-note">2012&ndash;2025 &middot; SPY 0.92</div></div>
<div class="metric"><div class="metric-value">1.58</div><div class="metric-label">Sharpe excluding 2020</div><div class="metric-note">the honest number</div></div>
<div class="metric"><div class="metric-value">&minus;17%</div><div class="metric-label">Max drawdown, simulated</div><div class="metric-note">SPY &minus;34% same window</div></div>
<div class="metric"><div class="metric-value">~44%</div><div class="metric-label">Average gross exposure</div><div class="metric-note">not fully invested</div></div>
</div>
```

::: {.note-strip}
Figures above are **simulated** results from a historical backtest over 2012–2025,
not live trading results. Simulated performance has inherent limitations: it is
constructed with hindsight, does not reflect the impact of real order flow, and does
not guarantee future results. A live track record is available on request.
:::

## The problem

Leveraged index ETFs decay in choppy markets. They rebalance daily, so the compounded
return depends on the path and not just the endpoint — a sideways market grinds them
down even when the index finishes flat. Holding one indefinitely is a bet that
volatility stays low.

Rime asks something narrower: can you hold that exposure only while the drag is small,
and be somewhere else the rest of the time?

## How it decides

The allocator is a shallow decision tree over three groups of inputs — a set of trend
and volatility state variables, a macro overlay, and a volatility circuit breaker.

The tree is shallow on purpose. Fourteen years of daily bars isn't a big sample, and
every extra split is another chance to fit noise.

The macro overlay leans on cross-asset series that tend to move ahead of equities
rather than alongside them. The circuit breaker cuts leveraged exposure when volatility
spikes, and it runs on hysteresis — the level that switches it on isn't the level that
switches it off — so the allocation doesn't thrash around a single threshold. On top of
that sits a rebalance deadband: if the target hasn't moved much, nothing trades.

::: {.note-strip}
The specific state variables, macro series, and thresholds aren't published here.
Happy to walk through them in an interview.
:::

## The engineering that matters

**One decision function.** Research and production call the same function. There's no
notebook that approximates what the live system does, because that gap is the usual way
a backtested strategy quietly stops being the strategy you tested. State persists
between runs, so the live system's view of the current regime survives a restart
instead of being rebuilt from a truncated window.

**Data quality gates.** Bad ticks, stale bars, and missing sessions get caught before
anything reaches the allocator. If the feed looks wrong, the system sits out.

**47 pytest tests** across the signal tree and the risk overlays — regime transitions,
breaker behavior at the hysteresis boundaries, deadband logic. Mostly they exist so I
can change things without guessing.

## Validation

One backtest number doesn't tell you much, so I put it through a few things that could
have killed it:

```{=html}
<table class="spec">
<tr><th>Walk-forward folds</th><td>Parameters fit on one window, evaluated on the next, rolling forward. No single global fit.</td></tr>
<tr><th>Pre/post-2020 splits</th><td>2020 is an outlier regime that flatters almost any volatility-responsive strategy. Reported separately for exactly that reason.</td></tr>
<tr><th>Slippage &amp; commission stress</th><td>Costs scaled well past realistic levels to find where the edge disappears.</td></tr>
<tr><th>Block bootstrap</th><td>Resampling in blocks to preserve autocorrelation, testing whether results depend on the specific historical path.</td></tr>
</table>
```

Both 1.86 and 1.58 are on this page because the gap between them is the finding. 2020
contributed a large share of the headline Sharpe, and quoting only the higher number
would be misleading.

## What I'd do next

- Swap the shallow tree for a probabilistic regime model, and check honestly whether it beats the rules instead of assuming it will.
- Model execution against intraday liquidity rather than assuming a fill at the daily close.
- Widen the macro overlay carefully. More inputs are more degrees of freedom.
